Summary: All reviewers (emMe, 1pd3, JaNm, and bmMJ) gave a rating of 4 or higher, with an unweighted average of 4.5. The discussion broadly demonstrates the value of the submission lies in the gaps it closes compared to other available datasets, in particular w.r.t. the population being sampled (geographically, ethnographically, skin type, and disease classes), the technical details and rigor, as well as the sophistication in the labeling. Some limitations remain, but the authors have, where necessary, addressed these to the extent necessary to accept this dataset for publication. The AC recommends to accept this submission as a poster (or, if the SAC/PC believe it to be of greater interest, then as a spotlight or oral presentation).

Strengths: The data collected covers skin types and granular, hierarchical disease classes that are grossly underrepresented in the extant literature. The labeling of the data was conducted in line with accepted standards, and so the dataset makes for an excellent addition for the community to improve on AI in the field of clinical-imaging based dermatological diagnostics (triage, practitioner support, XAI efforts, etc.). The protocol employed suggests the authors were aware of several pitfalls with prior efforts, and took them into account for this dataset.

Weaknesses: The authors admit in discussions that the heterogeneity of resolution is both an issue (training and inference steps from a technical perspective) and a potential benefit (heterogeneity creates more robust applications downstream). It would have been highly desirable to see some additional metadata fields (e.g., image cropping % in both axes, distance estimate between subject and lens in cm or inches, etc.) to support future applications that will likely benefit from this information. The exploratory analyses section of the paper leaves many aspects to the guesses of the reader -- the relatively low performance of the models (compared to recent published results from other datasets with similar models) could be due to a number of reasons, some of which may have to do with image collection protocol choices, which will have to be explored and addressed by future research; here the authors could have improved the most, but it is very understandable that this was not easily possible after the fact (given that some of the necessary metadata was not collected at image capture time). In addition, the authors could easily have explored additional tasks (segmentation, etc.) for the purpose of further demonstrating the value, again leaving this to the imagination of the reader. That all being said, these are labor intensive to study, and the AC is satisfied that the dataset as presented already creates sufficient additional value (and further investigative motivation and incentives for the field to devote significant resources in the prior underrepresented areas), for this to merit publication.

Featured reviewer comments:
- 1pd3: "First annotated dataset focused on Indian skin phototypes, filling a crucial gap [...]"
- 1pd3: "[...] board-certified dermatologist annotations [...]"
- 1pd3: "Introduction of concept bottleneck models for dermatology that leverage anatomical and morphological features"
- bmMJ: "[...] multi-dimensional annotations (e.g., lesion descriptors, body parts, hierarchical diagnoses), surpassing the granularity of existing dermatology datasets."
- bmMJ: "[the dataset] does not empirically validate whether these [skin tone] distributions match the true demographic diversity of South India. This limits claims about representativeness."
- bmMJ: "With 5,450 images, DermaCon-IN is smaller than some existing datasets (...), potentially restricting its utility for training large-scale models." -> rebuttal: "[...] despite its smaller size, DermaCon-IN offers significant value as a resource for fine-tuning large-scale models—particularly in improving generalisation to underrepresented populations." -> AC comment: given similar and (by an order of magnitude) smaller efforts in the DDI dataset (656 images available here: https://ddi-dataset.github.io/), I do believe the authors correctly assess the value of this effort w.r.t. the dataset's size
- emMe: "The data collection, Image acquisition protocol, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and annotation process are clear and well-documented, and decisions are well-supported throughout the main text."

Discussion: The authors respond to all points brought up by the reviewers, which mostly deal with (near) impossible to ameliorate issues related to data collection protocol choices, and naturally occurring limitations given the setting in which the data was collected (set of treatment centers limiting the variability of diseases and specific patient population covered). That being said, all reviewers set their final rating at 4 or higher, suggesting overall satisfaction with the process.

Dear Reviewers and AC,

We would like to thank all the reviewers for their constructive engagement and for recognising our focus on diverse regional disease patterns from the South Asian region, detailed skin tone distribution, and hierarchical, clinically validated labelling as key contributions, which we had envisioned as the novelty of our prospectively curated dataset. Across the reviews, there was a consistently positive and appreciative assessment of the work, acknowledging that, in addition to supporting interpretable medical AI, the dataset’s dual annotation system and detailed skin tone information make it valuable for fairness evaluation beyond medical applications.

Among the points raised, Reviewer bmMJ queried the dataset size. Existing datasets retrospectively curated from archival repositories may sometimes be larger than ours; however, our prospectively curated dataset captures natural variability (e.g., the long-tailed nature of disease occurrence), making it demanding for model development. After we explained its type and the prospective curation process in detail, the point was acknowledged in light of the quality-focused approach and the context of its development — a view also shared by Reviewer emMe.

We believe these characteristics position the dataset as a valuable resource for future clinical AI research in dermatology, with the potential to drive advances toward more equitable and clinically grounded AI.

Dear Reviewer 1pd3,

Thank you for your thoughtful review. We are encouraged by your recognition of the dataset’s contribution to addressing representation gaps in dermatology AI and the strength of our annotations and benchmarks. Below, we address the minor concerns raised:

1. **Resolution Heterogeneity**: We agree that variation in image resolutions poses a training challenge (section 5, line 238 of manuscript). However, we view this heterogeneity as an advantage. It reflects real-world variability in image acquisition, promoting the development of models that generalise better across diverse settings.
Training solely on fixed-resolution images from a single source may lead to lower generalisability and reduced deployment readiness. We addressed resolution differences using standard resizing techniques and acknowledge that future work may explore advanced augmentation strategies to further manage such heterogeneity.

2. **Concept Learning Issues:** We would like to respectfully clarify that this issue is acknowledged and discussed in the manuscript (Section 6.2, Qualitative Analysis, line 354). The observed variation in concept-class alignment across disease categories is expected and can be primarily attributed to:
 - class imbalance at the disease level, and
 - imbalance in instance-level concept distributions.

These challenges are inherent to real-world clinical datasets, especially in dermatology, where disease prevalence and visual patterns vary across populations, as discussed in Section 5 of the manuscript. To address this, we applied weighted sampling during CBM (Type 2) training, which improved concept-class alignment for minority classes. The table below summarises class-wise Spearman correlation scores (ρ) as computed using the alignment method described in the caption of Figure 10 in the manuscript. The table compares the alignment performance with and without weighted sampling, with classes ordered by sample size:
>| Class                          | # Samples | ρ (No Sampler) | ρ (Weighted Sampler) |
>|-|-:|-:|-:|
>| Infectious Disorders | 2,227     | **0.229**          | 0.139                 |
>| Inflammatory Disorders | 1,592     | 0.077          | **0.082**                 |
>| Pigmentary Disorders | 831       | 0.038          | **0.197**                 |
>| Skin Appendages Disorders | 480   | 0.052          | **0.151**                 |
>| Other Skin Disorders  | 159       | **0.147**          | 0.082                 |
>| Keratinisation Disorders | 72     | 0.184          | **0.256**                 |
>| Neoplasms and Tumors  | 52        | -0.044          | **-0.010** |
>| No Definite Diagnosis | 37        | **-0.083**         | -0.097                |

Weighted sampling consistently improves concept-class alignment for underrepresented and mid-sized categories (e.g., Pigmentary Disorders, Skin Appendages Disorders, Keratinisation Disorders), mitigating imbalance during concept learning. A decrease in alignment for the largest class (Infectious Disorders) suggests a trade-off introduced by rebalancing. 
Further, Section 7 of the manuscript outlines strategies like concept-weight normalisation to improve targeted alignment, supporting broader efforts to develop models suited for diverse, imbalanced datasets in real-world settings.

3. **Baseline Performance:** The best-performing model (Swin Transformer) achieves a mean accuracy of 70.41% on the 8-class Main Class task, reflecting the real-world complexity of dermatological diagnosis in our dataset. Collected from ~3,000 patients, the images exhibit significant visual heterogeneity and frequent multi-lesion presentations, posing clinical and modelling challenges. We present this result as a clinically meaningful benchmark highlighting the limitations of current deep learning models, including ViTs and CNNs, in handling such variability and underscores the need for future work on improved model design.


4. **More ablation studies:** We would like to clarify that Table 3 in the manuscript presents a focused ablation study analysing the impact of different concept annotation types on the classification performance of Main Class (MC) and Sub Class (SC) classification. We compare Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM) variants using:  
- Descriptors only (CBM‑D) for MC,  
- Body‑parts only (CBM‑B) for MC,  
- Both descriptors & body parts for MC and SC individually,  
- And two hierarchical CBM variants (Type 1 and Type 2), which jointly leverage SC and MC heads  

For the sake of completeness, we present the following ablations across: (i) descriptors alone, (ii) body parts alone for SC classification below:  
>| Class | Concepts               | Accuracy | Precision | Sensitivity | F1 Score | Macro AUC |
>|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
>| SC    | Descriptors & Bodyparts| 57.37 ± 0.01  | 57.67 ± 0.01     | 57.27 ± 0.01 | 56.90 ± 0.01   | 78.39  ± 0.02   |
>| SC    | Descriptors            | 56.42 ± 0.01  | 55.72 ± 0.01  | 56.51 ± 0.01 | 55.63± 0.01 | 80.16  ± 0.01  |
>| SC    | Bodyparts              | 55.88  ± 0.01  | 55.47  ± 0.01   | 55.90  ± 0.01   | 54.87  ± 0.01  | 78.94 ± 0.01  |

That said, if the reviewer has any specific suggestions or directions in mind, we would be grateful for the guidance and will incorporate them in the revised version.

5. **Multi-lesion images:** We would like to clarify that multi-lesion images in the DermaCon-IN dataset refer to the occurrence of a disease as multiple lesions, either localized at a single site or dispersed across different body regions. Such presentations are common in clinical practice and were deliberately included to reflect real-world diversity. The Swin Transformer was able to handle this complexity to some extent, which contributed to its relatively better performance, as discussed in Lines 277 and 289.

If the question pertains to images containing multiple distinct disease types, we would like to highlight that such cases are explicitly captured under the second-level subclass hierarchy through four dedicated subclasses representing co-occurring conditions. Although these multi-disease cases are relatively rare in clinical practice and seldom documented in existing dermatology datasets, their inclusion reflects our deliberate effort to build a high-fidelity benchmark that captures the nuanced realities of outpatient dermatological care.

To evaluate how our models handle these complex multi-disease samples, we conducted a targeted misclassification analysis using the best-performing Swin transformer. The following table summarizes this analysis: 

>| True Class                              | Predicted as Both | Predicted as Either                          | Predicted as Other          |
>|-|-|-|-|
>| Inflammatory + Infectious-Bacterial         | 5                      | Inflammatory (4), Bacterial (3)              | Pigmentary (1)               |
>| Fungal + Bacterial                          | 1                      | Fungal (3)          | Inflammatory (1)                                |
>| Parasitic + Bacterial                       | 3                      | Parasitic (2)                                    | Inflammatory (1)                 |
>| Inflammatory + Fungal                       | —                      | Fungal (2), Inflammatory (1)                             | —               |

We found that while a subset of samples were correctly classified into their corresponding multi-disease subclass (Predicted as Both), a considerable portion were predicted as one of their constituent disease types (Predicted as Either), likely reflecting the dominance of one pathology’s visual cues. Additionally, a smaller number of samples were predicted as unrelated classes (Predicted as Other). For instance, a sample labeled Inflammatory + Fungal was often predicted as Fungal when fungal-specific features were more visually prominent (e.g., scaly plaques).

We will include this discussion in Section 5. We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion.



6. **Figure 5:** We appreciate the feedback and will explain Figure 5 in greater detail by including the following description in the revised manuscript:

> This figure presents the chord diagrams of Pearson correlations between 8 main disease classes and two concept types: (A) disease descriptors and (B) body parts. In each chord diagram:
>- Ribbon width indicates the strength of association between a concept and the class (within-class correlation).
>- Ribbon color (dark blue to red) reflects the strength of correlation across all classes—dark blue for strong positive, red for negative.
>- Numeric values on ribbons denote the actual Pearson correlation coefficients.
>
>For example, in (A), under Pigmentary Disorders, the concept ‘White’ shows a moderately wide ribbon and a dark blue color with a correlation of +0.71, indicating a strong and distinct association both within the class and across all classes. In contrast, under Keratinisation Disorders, ‘Hyperkeratotic plaques’ has a wider ribbon (indicating strong within-class correlation) but a lighter blue color and lower correlation (+0.47), suggesting it is less distinctive across classes compared to ‘White’.

7. **Practical deployment considerations:** The primary focus of DermaCon-IN is to address representation gaps by capturing clinically realistic images from outpatient settings in South India, and to provide extensive baseline evaluations across classification and interpretability tasks. While the current work centres on dataset release and benchmarking, we agree that practical deployment in healthcare settings will require further efforts in model performance improvement and optimization. These considerations along with ethical diligence and deployment contexts, are discussed in Sections E and F of the supplementary material.


Thank you once again for your thoughtful reviews. We hope these clarifications address your concerns.

Dear Reviewer JaNm,

Thank you for your thoughtful and detailed feedback. We greatly appreciate your recognition of the paper's clarity, the rich annotations in our dataset, and the robust, multi-institutional data collection process. 

The extensive concept annotations in our dataset provided a unique opportunity to design a model that leverages these annotations for classification while assessing the model's faithfulness. ***Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs)*** were an ideal approach, allowing us to utilise textual information and move beyond basic interpretability.

In addition to CBMs, we thoroughly examined concept alignment with the model's decisions by incorporating Grad-CAM visualisations, offering a level of transparency that goes beyond traditional techniques such as saliency maps or attention visualisations.

Regarding ***semantic segmentation***, we fully agree that it is crucial in clinical imaging. However, the current version of DermaCon-IN does not include pixel-level masks, which are necessary for supervised segmentation. While weakly-supervised or concept-driven segmentation approaches could be explored, the lack of annotated segmentation masks limits objective evaluation and benchmarking. We recognise this as an important direction for future work and will consider it for potential dataset expansion.

We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the potential of ***generative modelling***, particularly given the rich concept-level annotations in DermaCon-IN. However, we believe that evaluating models directly on real-world clinical images, without incorporating synthetic data, provides a more accurate and unbiased assessment of the dataset’s current capabilities. In clinical settings, where diagnostic accuracy and robustness are essential, testing models with authentic data ensures that they are evaluated under conditions reflective of actual clinical scenarios.

That being said, we agree that generative modelling holds promise for future research. Given the importance of generating clinically realistic dermatological images for real-world outpatient applications, this remains a complex and non-trivial challenge due to the diversity of anatomical regions and the detailed visual descriptors involved, warranting further research exploration. We view generative modelling as a valuable future direction, offering opportunities to enhance the utility of DermaCon-IN.

Thank you once again for your valuable insights, and we appreciate your thoughtful evaluation of our work. Should you have any further questions or comments, we are happy to address them.

Dear Reviewer bmMJ,

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We appreciate your recognition of the dataset's rich annotations and efforts to address biases and diversity inclusion. We’re glad the benchmarking and interpretability models were well-received, and we value your acknowledgement of the dataset’s potential for both performance and interpretability research.
We would like to address your concerns in detail below:

**1. Skin Tone Distribution Validation:**  

We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding the need to better support the representativeness of skin tone distributions. We reference prior dermatological literature to ground our dataset in population-level evidence to address this. Studies in Dermatology and pigmentation consistently report that Fitzpatrick Skin Types (FST) III to VI are prevalent across the Indian population, with Types IV and V being most common, particularly in South Indian regions where higher UV exposure and geographic factors contribute to increased melanin levels [1, 2, 3]. These trends are well-recognised and support the presence of broad skin tone heterogeneity within this range, as illustrated in Figure 2.

In addition,  we refer to the work of Schumann et al. [4], which investigates the Monk Skin Tone (MST) scale and its application to demographic fairness evaluations. Their findings support the MST and FST scales as complementary frameworks [4, 5]. As illustrated in Figure 2 of the manuscript, our dataset spans MST 4 to 8, which aligns closely with mid-to-deep Fitzpatrick types, thereby providing robust coverage of representative Indian skin tones.

We will incorporate the following supporting references in the revised manuscript to more explicitly ground the dataset’s skin tone distribution in established population-level dermatological evidence:

>References:
>
>[1] S. Sachdeva. Fitzpatrick skin typing: Applications in dermatology. Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology, 75(1):93–96, 2009. https://doi.org/10.4103/0378-6323.45238
>
>[2] Sarkar R et. al and others. A randomised study to evaluate the efficacy and effectiveness of two sunscreen formulations on Indian skin types IV and V with pigmentation irregularities. **2. Limited Data Sources:** 

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding potential selection bias in the curation of dataset. However, we would like to clarify that multiple aspects of our data acquisition strategy mitigate this concern and support the broader generalizability of our dataset.

The dataset was primarily collected from three tertiary care hospitals and their affiliated regional clinics in South India. These institutions are located near state borders and are major referral centres for neighbouring regions. While IRB-approved ethical protocols and participant privacy considerations prevent us from disclosing individual-level demographic metadata, it can be broadly inferred that patients attending these centres come from a wide range of districts across Karnataka, Maharashtra, Goa, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh states. This diverse clinical base enhances the dataset’s representational depth, capturing substantial variation in disease presentation and skin tone, reflective of the broader dermatological caseload seen in South Indian outpatient care.
In addition, patient inclusion was voluntary and opportunistic, based on outpatient visits. Individuals from varied socioeconomic and regional backgrounds were invited to participate. There were no restrictions based on disease type, severity, age, or gender, resulting in a random and naturalistic sampling of dermatological cases typically seen in routine clinical practice, which reflects random population-level sampling in prospective cohort studies.

Importantly, the disease distribution observed in our dataset is consistent with the prevalence patterns reported in dermatological outpatient studies across South Indian states. Multiple region-specific epidemiological studies and OPD survey reports from neighbouring districts and states [2,3,4,5,6,7,1] support this clinical relevance, which consistently report a similar distribution of common skin conditions such as Fungal Infections, inflammatory disease, acne, pigmentary disorders, and eczema. **3. Moderate Dataset Size:** 

We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful observation regarding the size of the DermaCon-IN dataset. While it is true that DermaCon-IN contains fewer images than retrospective datasets like Fitzpatrick17k (from Atlases DermaAmin and Atlas Dermatologico) or HAM10000 (from dermatology department archives), it is one of the largest prospectively collected, open-access dermatology datasets sourced from real-world outpatient settings, which covers diverse skin disease spectrum.

We believe that the strength of DermaCon-IN lies in its clinical relevance, contextual depth, and population specificity. The prospective design of DermaCon-IN, along with standardized protocols for image capture and clinical annotation, ensures minimized label noise and greater consistency in diagnoses and metadata. In contrast, retrospective datasets like Fitzpatrick17k and HAM10000, which were compiled from secondary sources, are more prone to label inconsistencies and selection biases. Notably, Fitzpatrick17k [1] acknowledges up to 3% label noise in a random sample of 504 images, with incorrectly labelled images identified by board-certified dermatologists. Additionally, the HAM10000 dataset [2] does not explicitly report expert or doctor cross-validation of its labels. In contrast, all images in DermaCon-IN were labelled by board-certified dermatologists, ensuring good quality annotations. Further, Healthcare data, by its very nature, is scarce, and collecting it in prospective settings is time-consuming due to the systematic procedures, ethical considerations, and privacy preservation protocols involved in ensuring quality and consistency.

We believe that, despite its smaller size, DermaCon-IN offers significant value as a resource for fine-tuning large-scale models—particularly in improving generalisation to underrepresented populations. It complements larger, less-specific datasets by addressing gaps in regional and phenotypic representation, and contributes nuanced, context-rich data that is essential for real-world clinical AI applications.

Further, we are actively expanding the dataset, with secured IRB approval. Data collection is ongoing across additional clinical sites in India, and an updated version of DermaCon-IN will be released in a future iteration.

summary.value: This paper introduces DermaCon-IN, a dermatological image dataset specifically designed to address the underrepresentation of South Asian populations in dermatology AI research. The dataset comprises 5,450 high-resolution clinical photographs from approximately 3,000 patients collected from outpatient clinics in South India. Each image is annotated with hierarchical disease labels (8 main classes, 19 subclasses, and 245 specific diseases) following Rook's dermatology classification, along with 96 clinical concepts including 47 lesion descriptors and 49 anatomical locations. The authors benchmark various deep learning architectures including CNNs (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet), vision transformers (ViT, MaxViT, Swin), and Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) to establish baseline performance. The Swin Transformer achieved the best performance with 70.41% accuracy on main class classification. The dataset specifically targets the gap in representation of darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick types IV-VI) and regional disease patterns common in tropical settings.

strengths_contributions.value:
Major Contributions:

-Addressing Critical Representation Gap: First annotated dataset focused on Indian skin phototypes, filling a crucial gap in global dermatology AI resources where darker skin tones are significantly underrepresented
-Comprehensive Multi-concept Annotations: a dual annotation system with both anatomical locations and lesion descriptors, enabling interpretable AI models that mirror clinical diagnostic workflows
-Clinical Validity: Hierarchical labeling based on gold-standard Rook's classification, adapted for regional relevance with strong inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.84)
-Scale and Quality: 5450 high-resolution images with 245 distinct diagnoses, representing the full spectrum of conditions seen in South Asian outpatient settings

Technical Strengths:

-Data collection protocol with board-certified dermatologist annotations
-Dual skin tone assessment using both Fitzpatrick and Monk scales for better representation
-Statistical validation showing meaningful concept-disease correlations aligned with medical knowledge

Methodological strengths:

-Introduction of concept bottleneck models for dermatology that leverage anatomical and morphological features
-Hierarchical classification approaches (cascade vs. parallel) for exploiting taxonomic structure
-Demonstration of concept interpretability through Grad-CAM visualizations

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Minor weaknesses:

Resolution Heterogeneity: Variable image resolutions (296-4608 pixels) from different devices may introduce training challenges

Concept Learning Issues: Uneven performance across disease categories in CBMs, with some classes showing poor concept-class alignment

Baseline Performance: Best model achieves only 70.41% accuracy on 8-class classification, suggesting room for improvement

The paper could benefit from more ablation studies on the impact of different annotation types
Limited discussion on handling multi-lesion images and their impact on classification

Some figures (especially Figure 5) are complex and difficult to interpret

Limited discussion on practical deployment considerations and computational requirements

summary.value: The paper introduces DermaCon-IN, a new dermatological image dataset of over 5,450 clinical images from South India. A key innovation is its rich multi-concept annotations, including over 240 hierarchical diagnoses, 49 anatomical locations, and 47 lesion-level descriptors, all aimed at fostering interpretable and clinically aligned AI research. While benchmarking shows promising results with models like Swin Transformer for main class prediction, the study also highlights challenges such as the impact of facial anonymization and uneven concept-class alignment in interpretability models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper is well-written, well-organized and easy to follow.
2. The dataset includes rich multi-concept clinical annotations for interpretability: 49 precise anatomical locations and 47 lesion-level descriptors, supporting structured supervision and interpretable AI modeling by reflecting how dermatologists diagnose.
3. The data was collected prospectively through a multi-institutional collaboration, ensuring high-quality images and demographic diversity. The annotation process involved multiple board-certified dermatologists with robust quality control, achieving high inter-rater agreement.

limitations_weaknesses.value: While comprehensive, the benchmarking primarily focused on classification and basic interpretability, leaving more advanced tasks like semantic segmentation or generative modeling unexplored despite the dataset's rich annotations.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Good work. I do not have further concerns.

summary.value: The paper introduces DermaCon-IN, a new dermatological image dataset from the South Indian population. It offers over 5k images in which all samples has concept-level annotations such as body parts and disease descriptors.  The dataset also includes  sample-level information Fitzpatrick and Monk skin tones scales. Disease labels are organized in a three-tier hierarchy: main diagnostic class, etiology-based subclass, and specific disease label. Lastly, the paper presents baseline results including convolution and Transformers-based models and interpertability experiments with Concept Bottonecks Models (CMBs).

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper is easy to follow and, in general, well organized. It presents a dermatological image dataset sourced from South India and annotated by four specialists. Available labels include annotated anatomical locations and lesion-level descriptors that follow three-level disease taxonomy by Rook’s Classification. Each sample contains dense metadata: hierarchical disease labels, body parts, skin lesion descriptors, Fitzpatrick and Monk skin tone scores, diagnostic certainty, and image gradability.

Compared to prior work, the paper includes data from a broad skin disease spectrum instead of neoplasm and tumors (which are more common in the literature) sourced from South India and labeled by four Dermatologists with varying ranges of experience. Available information also includes the Fitzpatrick and Monk skin tone scale, which allows researchers to use it for fairness and skin tone-related research.  One of the main benefits is including only samples without missing annotations or meta-data.   

The data collection, Image acquisition protocol, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and annotation process are clear and well-documented, and decisions are well-supported throughout the main text.  

In general, the benchmarking is well organized and includes several convolution—and transformers-based deep learning models. The baseline models also include experiments with CBMs to leverage textual information.

limitations_weaknesses.value: I couldn't find many issues. The paper is easy to follow, but I have some suggestions: 1) Consider changing the section order: move Section 5, "Challenges and Opportunities," to follow Section 6, "Benchmarking with Models."; 2) Table 3 is somewhat difficult to understand at first glance. I recommend organizing the table into MC-based and SC-based groups for quicker visual assessment and comparison. ; 3) Please change the standard accuracy metric to balanced accuracy.

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is available at Harvard Dataverse website, including files to download all data, train/test splits and training and evaluation scripts.

In light of the author's comments and rebuttal, the dataset and its rich annotation are valuable for both the skin lesion, medical, and fairness communities. The benchmark itself is sound, and the paper has more positive reasons that outweigh the negative ones. My rating remains unchanged.

title.value: DermaCon-IN: A Multiconcept-Annotated Dermatological Image Dataset of Indian Skin Disorders for Clinical AI Research

TLDR.value: A richly annotated South Indian dermatological dataset featuring diverse diagnoses, skin tones, and detailed clinical concepts for advancing concept-driven AI models for dermatology.

abstract.value: Artificial intelligence is poised to augment dermatological care by enabling scalable image-based diagnostics. Yet, the development of robust and equitable models remains hindered by datasets that fail to capture the clinical and demographic complexity of real-world practice. This complexity stems from region-specific disease distributions, wide variation in skin tones, and the underrepresentation of outpatient scenarios from non-Western populations. We introduce DermaCon-IN, a prospectively curated dermatology dataset comprising 5,450 clinical images from 3,002 patients across outpatient clinics in South India. Each image is annotated by board-certified dermatologists with 245 distinct diagnoses, structured under a hierarchical, etiology-based taxonomy adapted from Rook’s classification. The dataset captures a wide spectrum of dermatologic conditions and tonal variation commonly seen in Indian outpatient care. We benchmark a range of architectures, including convolutional models (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet), transformer-based models (ViT, MaxViT, Swin), and Concept Bottleneck Models to establish baseline performance and explore how anatomical and concept-level cues may be integrated. These results are intended to guide future efforts toward interpretable and clinically realistic models. DermaCon-IN provides a scalable and representative foundation for advancing dermatology AI in real-world settings.
